# Background

## SAM Projects & Allocations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
SAM is the source of truth for who may compute, where, and how much:

- **Facilities** (NCAR, UNIV, CSL, …) contain **allocation types**
  (groups), which contain **projects**.
- Each project holds **per-resource allocations**: an amount, a time
  window (`startDate`/`endDate`), and an account status.
- Each machine is a **pair of SAM resources**: a CPU resource plus
  `"<machine> GPU"` (e.g. `Derecho` / `Derecho GPU`).
- Projects carry their **user membership** (`uid`, `username`).
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 5
graph TD
    F[Facility] --> AT[Allocation type]
    AT --> P[Project]
    P --> RA["Allocation<br/>(per resource)"]
    P --> U[Users]
    P ~~~ CP["Project<br/>(sub-project)"]
    CP -. parentProject .-> P
```
:::
::::

## SAM Payload — `fstree_access`

One JSON document per resource; the CPU and GPU endpoints return the same
project set with per-resource figures:

```json
{ "facilities": [
  { "allocationTypes": [
    { "name": "C_CSL", "fairSharePercentage": 100.0,
      "projects": [
        { "projectCode": "CESM0002", "parentProject": null, "active": true,
          "resources": [
            { "name": "Derecho", "allocationAmount": 465000000,
              "startDate": "...", "endDate": "...",
              "accountStatus": "Normal",
              "users": [ {"uid": 12345, "username": "..."} ] } ] } ] } ] } ] }
```

## SAM Project Trees

Projects nest via `parentProject` — and NCAR runs **two conventions, stored
identically** (a per-project amount per resource):

- Invariant (audited upstream): a root's own amount **is already its subtree
  total** under both conventions.
- Amounts are deliberately never deduplicated by the API — consumers must
  handle the trees.

| convention | how it looks in SAM | example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **shared pool** | every member carries the *same* amount — the whole pool | `NMMM0003` + members, all 36.5M |
| **subdivided award** | children hold distinct amounts carved out of the root's total | `CESM0002` 465M; children carve 442M *of it* |

## The SAM API — "SAMuel"

- HTTP basic auth; credentials come from the environment
  (`SAM_API_USER`/`SAM_API_PASS`/`SAM_API_URL` via a shared `sam_auth.py`) —
  never hardcoded.
- Responses are server-side cached; both tools take `--clear-cache` to purge
  first when freshness matters.

| endpoint | provides |
|:--|:--|
| `/v1/fstree_access/<resource>` | facilities → projects → allocations → users |
| `/v1/queue` | per-resource queue list + wallclock limits |
| `/v1/wallclock_exemption` | per-user, per-queue overrides |
| `/v1/admin/cache/refresh?category=flask` | purge the server response cache |

## The Big Picture

::: {.notes}
To run a job, a user must submit with `-A <project>` naming an active
project they belong to with an allocation on that resource — SAM provides
the facts, PBS enforces them.

How the artifacts actually reach the scheduler is the "SAM to PBS Pipeline"
section later on.
:::

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
graph LR
    SAM[(SAM API)]
    SAM --> S2S["samuel2sql.py"]
    SAM --> FST["fsparsetree_mr.py"]
    S2S --> DB[("ncar_accounting.db<br/>(SQLite)")]
    FST --> RG["resource_group<br/>(fairshare tree)"]
    DB --> ACC["accounting.PY<br/>queuejob hook"]
    DB --> WCL["wallclock.PY<br/>queuejob hook"]
    RG --> SCHED["PBS scheduler<br/>(HUP to reload)"]
    ACC --> PBS[PBS Professional]
    WCL --> PBS
    SCHED --> PBS
```

## PBS Fairshare Concepts

- The **fairshare entity is the project** (`qsub -A PROJ0001`), not the user.
- Entities live in a **tree** (`resource_group` file); every vertex gets an
  integer **share**.
- **Shares are compared only among siblings** — a vertex competes with its
  peers for their parent's slice; a constant scale factor across a level is
  invisible.
- Usage accumulates as jobs run and **decays** with the scheduler's
  configured half-life; jobs are then prioritized by each entity's
  usage-vs-entitlement.

::: {.notes}
See the Altair "Understanding fairshare" white paper (docs/) for the full
treatment; these slides only need the tree + sibling-relative shares + decay.
:::

## PBS Fairshare — the factor

$$
\text{fairshare\_factor} = 2^{-\left(\text{tree\_usage}/\text{perc}\right)}
$$

- **0.5 is equilibrium** (usage = share).
- `tree_usage` is **inherited along the whole path from the root** — an idle
  leaf under busy parents still lands near 0.5 (worked example in Backup).

| tree_usage / perc | factor | meaning |
|--:|--:|:--|
| 0 | 1.00 | used ~nothing of the entitlement |
| 1 | 0.50 | used exactly the fair share |
| 2 | 0.25 | used twice the share — decays fast |

## PBS Fairshare — `fairshare_usage_res`

Usage should accrue as a **fraction of machine capacity**, so saturating the
GPUs and saturating the CPUs count comparably:

$$
\text{usage} \mathrel{+}= \left( \frac{\texttt{ncpus}}{N_{cpu}} + \frac{\texttt{ngpus}}{N_{gpu}} \right) \cdot \texttt{walltime}
$$

- PBS compares usage only **relatively** — against entitlement, and among
  siblings — so scaling every job by a constant changes no ranking.
- But PBS accrues usage as an **integer**, so those raw fractions truncate
  toward zero. Fix: **multiply through by $N_{cpu}$** — same ranking, usable
  integers.

In `$PBS_HOME/sched_priv/sched_config` (Derecho: $N_{cpu}=318464$,
$N_{gpu}=328$):

```
fairshare_usage_res: ncpus*walltime + (318464/328)*ngpus*walltime
```

- Shares are built in the **same units**, so usage and entitlement stay
  comparable; the constants live in `capacities.json` and **must match
  `sched_config`**.

## The `resource_group` File

Four columns: `Vertex_name  fairshare_id  parent  #shares` — parents must
appear before children; PBS rejects a share of 0 (minimum 1).

```{bash}
#| echo: true
head -8 data/derecho.tree
```

- The single top vertex is named for the machine (PBS's `root` is implicit).
- Facilities carry SAM's policy percentages; deeper tiers follow below.

# Tooling — `samuel2sql.py`

## One Accounting DB per Machine

```
samuel2sql.py [--clear-cache] <machine> <outfile>
```

- Unified successor to three divergent per-cluster scripts (Casper's two-DB
  split + Derecho's merged variant).
- Fetches the machine's **CPU and GPU trees**, `/v1/queue`, and
  `/v1/wallclock_exemption`; emits **one SQLite DB** in the Derecho schema.
- Queue lists come from SAM — the old hardcoded per-cluster lists are gone.
- Robustness: output built in a temp file and **renamed atomically**; a
  machine with no GPU resource (HTTP 404) gets empty `gpu_*` tables; any
  other fetch failure is fatal.

## The Database — a Contract with the Hooks

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**CPU tables**

- `users` (uid, name)
- `projects` (code, active)
- `project_status`
- `projectusers` (uid ↔ pid)
- `queues` (queue, wallclocklimit)
- `wcoverride` (uid, queueid, seconds)
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
**GPU mirror tables**

- `gpu_projects`, `gpu_status`, `gpu_users`

**Row counts (Derecho):**

```{bash}
#| echo: false
cat data/accounting_counts.txt
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The schema is byte-identical to the deployed Derecho DB — it is an
external contract with the PBS hooks, changed only in lock-step (it even
retains a vestigial unused `resource` table).
:::

## How the Hooks Consume It

`accounting.PY` (queuejob) validates `-A`; **CPU vs GPU jobs branch on
`ngpus`** in the select statement, querying `projects`/`projectusers` or
`gpu_projects`/`gpu_users`:

```sql
select projects.code, project_status.code, projects.active
from projectusers
join project_status on status = project_status.id
join projects on projectusers.pid = projects.id
join users on projectusers.uid = users.uid
where users.name is ?
```

```{bash}
#| echo: false
head -8 data/accounting_lookup.txt
```

`wallclock.PY` reads `queues` for the per-queue limit and `wcoverride` for
per-user exceptions (`-1` = unlimited; `R|S|M<digits>` queues map to
"reservation").

# Tooling — `fsparsetree_mr.py`

## A Weighted, Multi-Resource Fairshare Tree

```
fsparsetree_mr.py [--rollup LEVEL] [--equalize LEVEL] [--clear-cache] <machine> <outfile>
```

Successor to the flat single-resource generator; three changes:

1. **Merges CPU + GPU** SAM resources into one tree per machine.
2. **Weights project leaves** by a capacity-normalized burn rate (instead of
   flat `1`).
3. **Mirrors SAM's project trees** into nested vertices (instead of
   flattening to peers).

## The Weighting Model

For project $p$ with CPU allocation $A_{cpu}$ over $D_{cpu}$ days and GPU
allocation $A_{gpu}$ over $D_{gpu}$ days:

$$
w(p) = \frac{A_{cpu}}{D_{cpu}} + \frac{N_{cpu}}{N_{gpu}}\cdot\frac{A_{gpu}}{D_{gpu}},
\qquad
\text{share}(p) = \max\!\left(1,\ \text{round}(w \cdot \text{scale})\right)
$$

- **Burn rate** — dividing by each allocation's own window compares projects
  on per-day entitlement, not raw totals.
- **Capacity normalization** — the $N_{cpu}/N_{gpu}$ factor mirrors
  `fairshare_usage_res`, so shares and usage are in the same units.
- Constants per machine in `capacities.json`
  (Derecho: $N_{cpu}=318464$, $N_{gpu}=328$).

## The Tree, from the Top

::: {.notes}
Percentages are sibling-normalized (share / sum of sibling shares) — the
ratio PBS actually applies, whatever the share source. That is why S_Staff
shows 100%: it is CISL's only child, even though SAM policy says 70. Boxes
also carry each group's project-account count. Real Derecho data; some
siblings elided for space — regenerate with ./refresh_data.sh.
:::

{{< include _tree_overview.qmd >}}

## Handling Project Trees

Flattening SAM's project trees to peers **double-counts**: a shared pool is
claimed once per member (14×), a subdivided award twice (root + children).

- On Derecho, flat vs nested: `N_Divisional` projects claimed **3.2 B vs
  379 M** (−88%); `C_CSL` **1.16 B vs 181 M** (−84%).

The fix needs no tree taxonomy — PBS compares shares **only among siblings**:

- Interior vertex **`<code>grp`** carries the project's **raw amount** (a
  root's amount is already its subtree total, under both conventions).
- A **self-leaf `<code>`** carries the **residual**, so the root's own jobs
  compete fairly with its children:

$$
\text{leaf}(X) = X.\text{amount} - \sum \text{amounts of } X\text{'s carve-out children}
$$

(a child is a carve-out iff its amount differs from $X$'s).

## Project Trees — a Subdivided Award

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
{{< include _tree_cesm.qmd >}}
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Interior `grp` vertices (blue) hold **subtree totals**.
- Self-leaves (yellow) hold the **residual**: `CESM0002`'s own jobs get
  59.7M of the 181M subtree — what it did not carve out to children.
- Sub-trees recurse (`CESM0028grp`).
:::
::::

## Project Trees — a Shared Pool

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
{{< include _tree_pool.qmd >}}
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Pool members all carry the pool amount → **peers split it evenly**.
- `NMMM0083` shares the same pool over a **shorter window** → burns
  faster by design (95M vs 36.5M).
- A member with no allocation of its own floors to PBS's minimum share
  of 1.
:::
::::

## Alternate Share Policies — `--rollup` / `--equalize`

- Roll-up **overrides** top-down policy and warns per override — e.g.
  `N_NSC 59% → 0.48%` exposes a policy reserve being flattened.
- *"All accounts equal, tree-wide"* is the explicit combination
  `--equalize leaf --rollup facility`.

| flag | effect |
|:--|:--|
| `--rollup group` | allocation-group shares = Σ of member weights (not SAM %) |
| `--rollup facility` | …facility tier too |
| `--rollup all` | telescopes to one flat allocation-proportional pool |
| `--equalize facility` | facilities peer-equal (6 → 16.67% each) |
| `--equalize leaf` | every project account weighs the same (count-based) |


# Job Sort

Prioritizing job execution.

## The End Goal

We want a single job priority sorting algorithm we can apply across queues:

```
priority_boost +
(queue_scale*priority_scale)*(1000*fairshare_factor +
                              1000*min(1.0, eligible_time/172800.0)**2)
```

- Jobs are prioritized primarily by **merit**: `fairshare_factor`, with a quadratic
  dependence on `eligible_time`.
- That merit is scaled by the job's **tier** (`priority_scale`) and its **queue**
  (`queue_scale`); `priority_boost` is a separate additive operator override.

This requires several changes vs. what we do today.

::: {.notes}
FIXME: rationale for the 172800 magic number above,
:::

## Getting there

Three new **custom resources** — set only by operators (`csgteam`) and `root`,
never requestable by users:

- **`priority_boost`** (default `0`) — an additive **operator override**, sized
  to swamp the formula. Replaces the `qalter -p` boost that overwrites `Priority`
  and destroys the tier. Use this feature for `-l job_priority=special`, `ampsrt`,
  and other hacks.
- **`queue_scale`** (default `1.0`, must stay `> 0`) — a per-queue **multiplier**
  on the merit, set as a queue `resources_default`: `>1` favors a queue, `<1`
  disfavors. A missing value binds to `0` and clobbers the job, so the default is
  load-bearing.
- **`priority_scale`** (default `1.0`) — the priority *tier* as a **multiplier**
  on `(fairshare + wait)`, stamped by the `job_priority` hook, so a premium job
  with poor fairshare can lose to a regular job with good fairshare.

Create with `qmgr -c "create resource <name> type=float, flag=r"`, give each a
server `resources_default`, then set them in hooks or via a manager's
`qalter -l` — invisible to users, alterable by `csgteam`.

## Who Sets What

No new machinery — the existing `job_priority` hook, per-queue config, and
server defaults already do this:

- The **`job_priority` hook** (queuejob) stamps `priority_scale` per tier
  instead of `j.Priority`, plus `priority_boost` for the gated `special` /
  `system` classes; ad-hoc boosts become a manager's `qalter -l priority_boost=N`.
- **`queue_scale`** is a per-queue `resources_default` in `qmgr-config`, exactly
  like `resources_default.ncpus` / `preempt_targets` today — no hook.
- **Server `resources_default`** gives every job the safe floor; a missing
  multiplicative factor binds to `0` and would clobber the job.

| resource | type | default | set by |
|:--|:--|--:|:--|
| `job_priority` | string, user-requestable | `regular` | user `-l job_priority=…` (hook-validated) |
| `priority_scale` | float, unrequestable | `1.0` | `job_priority` hook, per tier |
| `priority_boost` | float, unrequestable | `0` | hook (gated) + manager `qalter -l` |
| `queue_scale` | float, unrequestable | `1.0` | per-queue `resources_default` |

::: {.notes}
Today `derecho/hooks/job_priority.py` sets `j.Priority` by class: regular 200,
premium 300, economy 140, special 800 (gated: cisl_special_account, ampsrt, ssg,
csg), system 1023 (gated: ssg, csg), preempt/develop 0. The migration keeps the
same class parsing, group gates, and MODIFYJOB rejection, but stamps
`priority_scale` (1.0 / 1.4 / 0.7 / …) and `priority_boost` (special, system)
instead of `j.Priority`. Per-queue `resources_default` are already how
`qmgr-config` sets queue GPU counts and preempt targets, so `queue_scale` slots
in beside them.
:::

## The `by_queue` decision

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The plan**

- Flatten the **normal** queues to equal `Priority` + `by_queue: False` → the
  formula ranks CPU and GPU jobs head-to-head in one pool.
- `queue_scale` then **tilts** among those queues where warranted.
- Dev/preempt keep a **higher, hard queue `Priority`** — a latency guarantee the
  formula can't (and shouldn't) override.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The catch (OpenPBS testbed)**

- Queue `Priority` is a **primary sort key the formula can't cross**.
- `by_queue: False` only merges queues **already equal** in `Priority`.
- Letting the formula arbitrate means **flattening** `Priority` — but
  `preempt_queue_prio` reads the same values, so preemption reshuffles.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Measured on the OpenPBS 23.06 testbed (2026-08-19); the clusters run PBS Pro
2024.1, so confirm there. Three queue pairs, each giving the lower-Priority queue
a formula score of 999 vs 10: cpudev(200) vs cpu(100) and cpu(100) vs pcpu(50)
both sorted by queue Priority under by_queue True *and* False; only the
equal-Priority cpu(100) vs gpu(100) pair flipped to formula order under
by_queue False. So queue_scale only bites among queues flattened to equal
Priority, and flattening them moves the preemption classes.
:::

## Open questions for the vendor

Our evidence is an OpenPBS 23.06 testbed; the clusters run **PBS Pro 2024.1** —
we'd like to confirm each of these there:

- **`sched_config` keys** — seven keys (`backfill`, `half_life`, `preempt_*`,
  `log_filter`) are no longer read from the file in 23.06; a stale value is
  **silently ignored**. Still file-read in 2024.1, or `qmgr`-only now?
- **Queue `Priority` vs. the formula** — can the formula ever outrank queue
  `Priority`, or must we flatten it (and disturb `preempt_queue_prio`)?
- **Formula failure modes** — confirm a missing custom resource binds to `0`
  (not a zeroed formula), while an unknown symbol or `^` fails at *evaluation* —
  silently, on every job.
- **Formula syntax** — `min()` / `max()` / ternary / `**` and `math` functions,
  and the `qmgr` quoting they need.

::: {.notes}
Testbed detail (2026-08-19): `^` is XOR in Python — `...^2` passes qmgr
validation, then raises for every job forever with only a DEBUG2 trace. A missing
consumable resource binds to literal 0, so the rest of the formula still
evaluates. A manager who is not root can `qalter` a resource users cannot
request. A custom resource can't be deleted while any job — including one in
history — still carries it, which shapes the rollback path.
:::



# Tooling — SAM to PBS Pipeline

## How Data Flows from SAM to PBS

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Updating PBS Artifacts — CSG**

- A `cron` process
- Can run on any node with access to `sam.hpc.ucar.edu`
- Rebuilds both artifacts, for every machine:
  - `resource_group` — the fairshare tree
  - `ncar_accounting.db` — projects, users, queues
- **Publishes only when the content changed**
- Touches no scheduler — cannot disturb a running system
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Updating PBS Scheduler — HSG**

- An admin, on the scheduler host
- Needs the privilege to pause and `HUP` the scheduler
- `make` against the published directory
- **Installs only what differs from what is deployed**
- A database swap is free; a tree costs a scheduler pause
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The published directory is the interface between the two groups — the one
place both sides touch. Each side gates on content independently rather than
trusting the other's bookkeeping, so the expensive action only ever happens
when something real moved.
:::

## SAM to PBS Schematic

::: {.notes}
Two artifacts, two independent gates, two very different consequences. The
database can be swapped under a running scheduler; the tree cannot, which is
the whole reason the pipeline refuses to act on unchanged content.

The common case by far is that both gates say "no" — the grey terminal — and
nothing anywhere is written or restarted.
:::

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
graph LR
    SAM[(SAM API)] --> CRON["CSG &middot; cron<br/>every 12 min"]
    CRON --> S2S["samuel2sql.py"]
    CRON --> FST["fsparsetree_mr.py"]
    S2S --> GD{"changed?"}
    FST --> GT{"changed?"}
    GD -. no .-> ND(["nothing published"])
    GT -. no .-> NT(["nothing published"])
    GD == yes ==> PDB[("ncar_accounting.db")]
    GT == yes ==> PTR[("resource_group")]
    PDB --> IDB["HSG &middot; rename into place<br/>no outage"]
    PTR --> ITR["HSG &middot; pause &rarr; install<br/>&rarr; HUP &rarr; resume"]
    IDB --> PBS["PBS Professional"]
    ITR --> PBS

    classDef handoff fill:#ffffff,stroke:#333333,stroke-width:3px
```

## Updating PBS Artifacts

- Runs from `cron.hpc.ucar.edu` every 12 minutes, via a wrapper that `ssh`es
  to a login node — **Casper, falling back to Derecho** only if `ssh` cannot
  reach it. Which node runs it does not change the result.
- Rebuilds the tree and database for every machine, validates them, and
  **replaces a published file only when its digest changed**.
- Digests are asymmetric on purpose: the tree by **bytes**, the database over
  its logical `.dump` — otherwise a `sqlite` upgrade would move every byte and
  trigger a pointless deploy on every cluster.
- A **churn guard** blocks an implausible delta — a collapsed table, wholesale
  membership churn — until a second run agrees, and exits non-zero so `cron`
  mails somebody.
- Each replaced artifact is kept as `<name>.prev`: plain `diff` for the tree,
  `sqlite3 .dump` for the database.

::: {.notes}
First day in production: ~70 cycles, the databases changed a handful of times
and the fairshare tree twice — every other cycle wrote nothing at all. That
ratio is the whole justification for content-gating.

One cycle failed on a transient SAM connect timeout: Casper published nothing
and kept its last good artifacts, Derecho published normally, and cron mailed
on the non-zero exit.

It never passes `--clear-cache` — that cache is shared with every other SAM
consumer.
:::

## Updating PBS Scheduler

HSG territory: this is the only half that can disturb a running scheduler.

```bash
make status                # what differs from what is deployed
make deploy                # install only that
make rollback-derecho      # put back the previous artifact
```

- Compares against **the deployed file itself**, not a timestamp — so it is
  correct on a fresh checkout, and it repairs a hand-edit or a partial copy on
  the next run instead of never noticing.
- **Database**: written as a sibling, then renamed over the destination.
  Atomic, no outage, safe while the hooks are reading it.
- **Fairshare tree**: pause scheduling → install → `HUP` → resume. The
  expensive path, and the reason everything upstream is content-gated.
- The `Makefile` is self-contained — copy it to the scheduler host, set the
  destinations and the pause/HUP/resume commands, and it needs nothing else:
  no checkout, no Python.
  - Today at `/glade/work/benkirk/repos/hpc-scheduling-tools/integration/`,
    alongside a `README.md` covering every failure mode
- **Casper deploys stay gated** until its hook migration lands.

::: {.notes}
Why the rename is safe under a live hook: a reader either holds a descriptor on
the old inode (complete, stale) or opens the new one (complete) — never a torn
file. Never unlink the destination, though: `sqlite3.connect()` on a missing
path *creates* an empty database, and every job would then be rejected with
"Invalid account".
:::

## When Something Looks Wrong

Most of these clear themselves; the table says which.

| you see | it means |
|:--|:--|
| `NOT PUBLISHED -- rerun to confirm` | churn guard tripped once; a legitimate delta publishes on the next run |
| `refresh: FAILED for <machine>` | transient SAM error; that machine keeps its last good artifacts, the others still publish |
| `REPAIRED <name>` | a published artifact had drifted and was restored — the content itself did not change |
| `fetch: verification failed` | the copy straddled a publish; one retry is automatic |
| `make status` says `DIFFERS` right after a deploy | the destination was edited out of band; the next `make deploy` repairs it |
| nothing changed for hours | normal — this is the common case |

::: {.notes}
`checked_at` in `status.json` answers "is the job alive"; `changed_at` answers
"did the data move". Conflating the two is the easy mistake — a long run of
unchanged cycles is health, not staleness.
:::

  `./refresh_data.sh` (`tree2mermaid.py` + `data/`).

## Observability — `fairshare_factor.sh`

For every project with queued jobs, computes
$2^{-(\text{tree\_usage}/\text{perc})}$ live on the PBS host and prints a
sorted table (8-way parallel `fairshare` queries).

Findings from a 212-project run:

- **Nothing scores above ~0.455** — reaching 1.0 needs the *entire* root
  path under-used, and the big facility tiers run at/above their shares.
- The bottom of the table spans ~60 orders of magnitude (tiny share, huge
  inherited usage → factor underflows toward 0).

## Worked Example — `tree_usage` Is Inherited

`SCSG0002`: raw own usage of **16 core-seconds**, yet:

```
Percentage           : 1.307190%
fairshare_tree_usage : 0.015112     <- inherited from CISL -> S_Staff
ratio = 1.156  ->  factor = 0.45
```

An idle leaf under busy parents cannot pull its tree-usage below its
parents' — by design: the group, not just the leaf, has spent its share.

## Verification Recipes

Structural checks on a generated tree (run here against the frozen copy):

```{bash}
#| echo: true
# duplicate vertex names (must be empty):
awk '{print $1}' data/derecho.tree | sort | uniq -d
# every parent defined before use (must be empty):
awk '{seen[$1]=1} $3!="root" && !($3 in seen){print "unordered:",$1}' data/derecho.tree
# shares are a real distribution, not all 1:
awk '{print $4}' data/derecho.tree | sort -n | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
```

`samuel2sql.py` was validated against the legacy builders: schema identical;
row-for-row identical tables except 11 intentionally-fixed GPU-only users.
